Plate book

Seven candidate figures for the benchmark battery — three ways to draw the structures, four ways to draw the convergence — plus one live explorer. Everything here is rendered from the real repository data, so whatever you pick is already most of the way built.

13 structures 5 code+rule columns 1 345 measured solves 1 … 961 retained orders λ = 1, lengths in µm

Grade them by their plate code — S1 S2 S3 for the structures, C1 C1t C2 C3 C4 X for the convergence. Keep, kill, or “keep but change …”. Click any figure to inspect it full size.

Part A

Drawing the structures

The battery spans three dimensionalities, and they do not want the same picture. A planar stack is fully described by a column of layers; a lamellar grating is fully described by one x–z cut; a pillar array is not — a cut through a square pillar and a cut through a cylinder are the same drawing. So the question is not “2D or 3D” globally, it is which view is complete for which case.

S1cross-section

Dimensioned x–z cut, mechanical-drawing style

Each panel at its own scale with a λ bar for calibration, thickness dimensioned in the right margin with extension lines, the beam glyph carrying the polarization, and — for the 2D cases only — the x–y top view the cut physically cannot show.

click to enlarge · 2185 × 1782
Reads
Exact geometry. Every number in structures.py is on the page and measurable against the λ bar.
Costs
The 2D cases need two sub-panels to be honest, which makes their rows busier than the 1D ones.
Best for
A reference plate in the README, and the figure you point at when someone asks “what exactly did you simulate?”
S23D cut-away

Isometric unit cell, faces textured with the real mask

Not a sketch: the top face carries the actual x–y rasterization, the front face the x–z cut, the side face the y–z cut. One picture is simultaneously the 3D view, the top view and the cross-section. Free-standing cases get a phantom half-space instead of a solid substrate, and E is drawn along the axis the polarization really selects — so TE-along-the-grooves versus TM-across-them is visible as geometry.

click to enlarge · 2185 × 1897
Reads
Instant. Square pillar versus cylinder versus hole array separate at a glance, and the polarization stops being a letter you have to decode.
Costs
Dimensions are harder to read off than in S1 — the isometric foreshortening is honest but not measurable.
Best for
The top of the README and any talk slide. The one that makes the battery legible to someone who has not read the code.
S3atlas

One shared length scale, sorted by period

Every row shows the same 3.3 λ-wide window, so how many periods you see is the sub-wavelength/diffracting story — and thicknesses are on that same scale too. A2 fits sixteen periods in the window; B1 fits two. That is the whole physics of the battery in one glance, and no per-panel scale bar can substitute for it.

click to enlarge · 2065 × 1014
Reads
Comparative. The only plate where you can see that C2 and B2 are nearly the same period but wildly different materials.
Costs
No per-structure detail — it is a contact sheet, not a spec sheet. It complements S1/S2 rather than replacing either.
Best for
The opening figure of the benchmark README, above the per-case plates.

What I would actually ship

Not one of them — a dimensionality-adaptive rule, because the three cases genuinely differ in what a complete description is:

  • 0D (A1, A1b) — a layer-stack column with the n(z) step profile beside it. A cut adds nothing; there is nothing to cut.
  • 1D (A2, B1, B2, B3, D1) — the S1 x–z cut, and nothing else. It is already the complete description of the structure.
  • 2D (C1, C1b, C2, D2) — the S2 isometric cut-away, which carries the top view and the cross-section on its own faces instead of needing a second panel.
  • All 13 together — S3 as the opener, once, on the shared scale.

That is one benchmark/structviz.py with a draw(structure) that dispatches on dim, and one plot_structures.py that emits the atlas plus the per-case sheet. Tell me if you would rather have a single uniform style for all thirteen instead.

Part B

Drawing the convergence

The current conv_*.png figures answer “what is R at this order?”. That is not the question the night run exists to settle. The questions are: does this rule converge at all, how many digits does it buy per millisecond, and do the codes agree with an independent reference. Four plates, each aimed at one of those. All four drop the red/green encoding — colour now means the factorization rule (the physics), dash and marker mean the codebase.

C1digit map

Convergence as correct digits, as a heat strip

One row per code+rule, one colour step per correct digit of R. A rule that never turns yellow never converges — and you see that without reading a single axis. The ▼ marks the first sustained |ΔR| ≤ 1e-4. C1 puts truncation order on x; C1t puts wall time on x, which is literally “convergence over time”.

C1 — versus retained orders · click to enlarge
C1t — versus wall time · click to enlarge
Reads
Fastest glance of anything here. Group C is visibly a wall of blue — nobody converges — and D1 is visibly Li and NV going yellow while both Laurents stay dark.
Costs
You lose the sign of the error and the shape of the decay. It tells you whether and when, never how.
Best for
The summary figure at the top of the convergence section, replacing nothing — it is the index to the other plates.
C2cost staircase

The best error a wall-time budget can buy

The replacement for conv_accuracy_vs_time.png. Faint markers are the raw measurements; the thick step is the running best — the honest answer to “if I have 100 ms, how close can I get?”. Monotone by construction, so the oscillation that makes the current figure unreadable becomes a flat tread instead of a scribble. A flat step means spending more time buys nothing.

click to enlarge · 1960 × 1523
Reads
The Ikarus-buys-back-its-cost result, directly. On B2 and D1 the blue and green staircases sit two decades left of the orange one at equal accuracy.
Costs
The envelope hides non-monotone behaviour on purpose. Keep the raw markers visible so it stays honest.
Best for
The figure the README's “time-to-accuracy” table is currently doing in prose.
C3scoreboard

What each rule costs to reach 1e-4, in orders and in milliseconds

Eleven cases, two panels, the same ranking read two ways. Hollow markers are lone crossings (provisional); ✗ in the right-hand lane means the sweep never got there. This is the whole of conv_convergence.csv as one picture.

click to enlarge · 1980 × 1008
Reads
A verdict. Both Laurent columns are ✗ on six of eleven cases; Li and NV are the only pair that lands on nearly every settled case.
Costs
One tolerance only. Everything about the approach — rate, sign, oscillation — is thrown away to get the ranking.
Best for
The headline figure. If only one convergence plot survives, this is the one that answers the question the benchmark was built to ask.
C4Moose, redesigned

Signed deviation from the independent reference, on a symlog axis

The current pair moose_compare_raw.png + _tight.png exists because one linear axis cannot hold both the low-order transient and the 1e-4 endgame. A symlog y-axis holds both: outside ±1e-4 it is logarithmic and you read the transient and the sign of the approach; inside the band it goes linear and the endgame is legible in the same panel. Moose stays black, as it should. The strip underneath is the summary — how far each code still is from the independent reference when the sweep ends.

click to enlarge · 1960 × 1366
Reads
One figure replaces two, and the sign is back — you can see Laurent crawling in from above rather than just “being wrong”.
Costs
A symlog axis needs its threshold explained once. After that it is the axis this data always wanted.
Best for
Replacing moose_compare_raw, _tight and _error with a single plate.
Part X · live

Every plate above is a fixed choice of axis. This is the same night-run data with the axis as a control — switch what y means and what x means and watch the same curves re-tell the story. Reply with plate codes. Anything you keep, I build properly into benchmark/ — as modules with the same style contract the existing plotters use, wired into plot_conv.py / plot_moose.py, regenerated against night_run_2, and committed to the branch.

Two things I need you to decide, not guess

  • Colour semantics. Every plate here encodes rule as colour and codebase as dash, on the argument that the physics story is direct-versus-faithful. The existing plotters do the opposite — colour is the codebase. Both Laurent columns therefore collapse to one grey here, which is a claim: the direct rule behaves identically in both codes. Keep the new encoding, or keep continuity with the old figures?
  • Structure style, one or three. The adaptive rule above gives 1D a flat cut and 2D an isometric — visually inconsistent across one sheet, but complete for each case. A single uniform style is prettier as a set and lies slightly about the 2D cases.
